transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, it’s... it’s kind of a long story, to be honest, but I guess the main thing is that things just got really, really out of hand at work lately. I do landscaping, you know, groundskeeping stuff. I’ve always just been a normal crew guy—show up, do the edging, lay the mulch, load the trucks, and go home. Nothing crazy. 

But recently, I just... I don't know, I got this huge idea for this park project and I went completely overboard with it. I mean, I went from being just a regular guy on the crew to suddenly trying to run three different commercial bids all by myself at the exact same time. I was on the phone constantly, calling city people, trying to track down the local zoning guys, aggressively lining up wholesale plant suppliers from all over the place to get pricing on trees we didn't even have a contract for yet. 

And it wasn't just at work, either. I was messaging literally everybody I knew—my boss, my coworkers, friends I haven't talked to since high school—just sending them these massive, endless walls of text about this park idea, the layout, the native plant species we could use, the irrigation plans, everything. It was like I just couldn’t shut it off. I was just locked onto getting all these things done and making this massive project happen right that second, and I couldn't stop pushing it and planning it. It just felt like I had to keep calling and organizing and messaging everyone until it was real, and... yeah, it was a lot.
Did you feel unusually happy or excited during this period when you were working on the park project?

Happy? I mean... I don't know if happy is exactly the right word for it, but excited, yeah, definitely excited. Honestly, before I crashed and everything just completely fell apart on me, I felt so fired up. It was like I had this electricity just buzzing right under my skin, and I felt... I don't know how to explain it, almost bigger than myself, if that makes any sense? Like I was finally doing what I was meant to do and I had this massive vision that nobody else could see yet. It was this huge rush. 

But the thing is, it wasn't just all good vibes and smiles, you know? Because I was so locked in on getting it done, if anyone got in my way... man. Like, if one of the other guys on the crew, say, if they even just questioned my plan for a second or told me I needed to slow down and take a breath, I would just absolutely snap. And I mean I’d snap at him way, way harder than made any sense at all for the situation. I'd just bite their heads off. They were probably just being normal, you know, just trying to figure out why the guy who usually just edges the sidewalks is suddenly acting like he owns the whole landscaping company, but I just had zero patience for it. I felt like they were dragging their feet and ruining this perfect momentum I had going, so if anyone tried to pump the brakes on me, I just got so incredibly ticked off at them. So yeah, I was definitely fired up, but it was a really intense kind of fired up.
Did you have any trouble sleeping during this period when you were working on the park project?

Trouble sleeping? Man, I... I don't really think so? I mean, I don't remember having a hard time with it, if that's what you're asking. 

Usually, if I can't sleep, it's just 'cause my lower back is absolutely screaming from throwing around fifty-pound bags of topsoil or river rock all day, but during that whole stretch with the park project... I don't know, I haven't really noticed any specific problems with my sleep. Like, I don't remember lying there staring at the ceiling fan for hours or tossing and turning and getting all frustrated. I'd be in bed, and my phone would be right there on my nightstand—I actually made that nightstand myself out of some reclaimed oak we pulled from a demo job a couple years back, sanded it down and stained it and everything—but anyway, I’d be in bed, and yeah, my brain was definitely still chewing on the irrigation layouts and whether we should go with the red maples or the dogwoods for the main walkway, but I don't recall actually fighting to fall asleep. 

It’s all kind of a blur, to be honest with you. I just remember being in my room, the window AC unit kicking on and off, my dog Buster snoring away at the foot of the mattress like he always does... so no, I wouldn't say I had trouble. I mean, unless you mean something else by trouble? Because I know guys who wake up at like 2 AM every single night and just have to go sit in the living room and watch TV. My crew boss Mike, he does that, says his brain just won't let him stay in bed. But I wasn't doing anything like that. I don't really have anything to tell you on the sleep front, honestly. I just don't remember it being an issue.
Did you feel like you were more important or capable than usual during the time you were working on the park project?

Yeah, I did. I really, really did. It’s almost embarrassing to think about it now, sitting here, but at the time? Man, I felt like I was completely untouchable. Like I had suddenly unlocked this level of my brain that nobody else even knew existed. 

I mean, look at me. I’m a guy who edges sidewalks and hauls mulch for a living. I barely scraped through high school, and most weeks I’m just trying to make sure I can cover my rent and keep my truck running. But during those couple of weeks with the park project... I honestly believed I was about to become *the* guy. Like, the absolute top-tier expert that every single town and city council in a fifty-mile radius was going to be calling up for sustainable landscaping. 

I remember sitting in my truck one afternoon—I had just finished eating a gas station sandwich, totally normal day—and I was looking at this empty dirt lot near the highway, and I just saw the whole thing. The grading, the drought-resistant grasses, the exact placement of the retaining walls. And I thought to myself, "I am the only person who can see this. I’m a visionary." I genuinely thought I was going to bypass my boss, bypass the guys who actually own the company, and just start landing these massive, million-dollar municipal contracts all on my own. I was already planning out how I was going to hire my own crews, what the logo for my new empire was going to look like, how I was going to revolutionize the way public parks were designed in this state. 

And the crazy part is, it didn't feel like a daydream. You know how sometimes you daydream about winning the lottery or whatever? It wasn't like that. It felt like a stone-cold fact. I felt so incredibly capable, like every thought I had was just pure gold and everyone else was just moving in slow motion. I felt like I was ten feet tall and made of steel, just... destined for this massive, important life, even though in reality, I’m still just trying to keep my small jobs paid up and not get fired for snapping at my crewmates. But right then? Yeah. I felt like the most important guy in the room, no matter what room I was in.
Was this feeling of being fired up and excited present every day during the time you were working on the park project?

Yeah, yeah, it was. Every single day. It wasn't just like a good mood that comes and goes, you know? Like sometimes you wake up and the sun's shining and you had a good cup of coffee and you feel great for a few hours until you hit traffic or something. It wasn't like that at all. 

It started right when I got this idea in my head that I was going to remake myself, right before I started putting together that whole pitch for the park project. I remember I went to the hardware store—the big one over on Route 9, not the local one because they never have the specific drafting pencils I suddenly decided I needed—and I bought all these notebooks and grid paper, and from that exact moment, the switch flipped. And once it flipped, it stayed stuck in the 'on' position. 

For about two solid weeks, from the minute I opened my eyes in the morning to whenever I finally crashed out at night, I was just running on that same high-voltage current. Every day on the job site, every evening sitting at my kitchen table drawing up those plans, every time I talked to anybody. It was just this constant, buzzing, fired-up feeling, day in and day out, for those whole two weeks. There wasn't a single dip in it. I mean, until the very end, obviously, when the bottom just completely fell out and I crashed harder than I ever have in my life. But yeah, for that two-week stretch? It was non-stop. Every day.
Did you feel like you needed less sleep than usual during those two weeks when you were working on the park project?

Less sleep? Well, like I was saying before, I didn't really have trouble sleeping, but... I mean, needing less? I don't know, honestly. I don't really remember thinking, "Oh, I need less sleep right now." 

It’s just... when you're in that zone, when your brain is firing on all cylinders like that, sleep just doesn't really factor into the equation in the same way. Like, I’d be at my kitchen table, right? The one with the wobbly leg that I keep meaning to fix with a matchbook or a piece of cardboard, but I never get around to it. I’d be sitting there, and I’d have my grid paper spread out, and my drafting pencils, and I'd be sketching out these massive, elaborate irrigation systems, color-coding the different zones for the drip lines versus the sprinkler heads, calculating water pressure drops... and I’d look up, and it would be 3 AM. And I’d think, "Man, I should probably get in bed," because I had to be at the yard by 6:30 to load up the trailers for the day's jobs. 

So I'd go to bed, and like I said, I don't remember tossing and turning or fighting it, but I don't really know how much I actually slept, or if I felt like I *needed* less. I just know that when 5:30 rolled around and my alarm went off, I was up. Boom. Feet on the floor, ready to go. I didn't feel groggy, I didn't hit snooze five times like I usually do when I'm just dragging myself through a normal week. I just got up, made my coffee—black, no sugar, just straight fuel—and I was out the door. 

But did I feel like I *needed* less? I’m not sure I ever stopped to analyze it like that. I was just moving so fast, you know? The momentum was so intense that sleep was just this brief pause button I had to hit before I could get back to the real work, the important stuff. I wasn't sitting there thinking, "Wow, I only got two hours of sleep and I feel great, I must need less sleep." It was more like, "Okay, the sun's up, time to go revolutionize the landscaping industry." So, I don't know if that answers your question. I just don't have a clear memory of feeling a decreased *need* for it, just that it wasn't the main event, if that makes sense.
Did you feel anxious at any point during those two weeks when you were working on the park project?

Anxious? No... no, not at all. I mean, usually, sure. On a normal day, I’ve always got this sort of low-level hum of worry going on in the background, you know? Like I was saying about my truck, it’s got this thing where the transmission slips if I accelerate too fast, and I’m always sweating over whether today is the day it finally blows out completely while I’m hauling a full load of river rock or something. Or I’m worrying about making rent, or if the boss is gonna cut my hours because it rained three days in a row and we can't run the mowers. 

But during those two weeks? Man, anxiety wasn't even in my vocabulary. 

Anxiety is what happens when you doubt yourself, right? When you think you might mess up or that things might go wrong. But I didn't have a single doubt in my head. Not one. I remember my buddy on the crew, Dave—he saw me sketching out some of the retaining wall specs on the back of a work order during my lunch break, and he was like, "Dude, aren't you worried the boss is gonna catch you planning your own side-hustle on company time?" And I just laughed at him. I literally just laughed out loud, because the idea of being scared of my boss just seemed completely ridiculous. I was sitting there thinking, "Why would I be worried about a guy who just cuts grass when I'm about to revolutionize the entire municipal park system?" 

So, no, I didn't feel nervous, I didn't have that tight, panicky feeling in my chest, none of that. I just felt completely bulletproof. It was like I was wrapped in this armor of absolute certainty. Every decision I made, every line I drew on that graph paper, I just knew it was a hundred percent correct. You can't be anxious when you know you're destined to win, you know? It just doesn't compute. So yeah, no anxiety at all. Just pure, solid confidence.
Was there ever a point during the day when you didn't feel excited or fired up about the park project?

Well, no, the fire was always there. It never went out. But... I guess it didn't always look like happy excitement, if that makes sense? Like, before I finally crashed, I just felt so fired up all the time, like I was literally bigger than myself. Like my physical body couldn't even contain all the ideas and the energy I had bouncing around inside me. I felt like a giant walking around all these regular people. 

But the thing is, when you feel that huge and that important, you don't really have patience for anyone who isn't on your level. So if there was a moment where I wasn't just cheerfully excited, it was because someone got in my way. Like, we were laying down this heavy-duty mulch over at the commercial park on 4th Street—the one with the terrible drainage that we have to fix every spring—and I was just hauling bags, moving at lightspeed, totally consumed by my park project plans. And one of my coworkers, Kevin—he’s this older guy, always complaining about his knees—he told me to slow down. He actually told me to slow down, and then he made some offhand comment questioning if my park plan was even realistic, like, "Who's gonna fund that, kid?" 

Man, I just snapped. I snapped at him way, way harder than made sense. I mean, normally I’d just roll my eyes at Kevin, but right then? I went off. I started yelling at him right there in the flowerbeds, telling him he was just a small-minded dirt-pusher who was never going to amount to anything, and that I was building a legacy. I was so furious. It was like that same fired-up energy just instantly turned into this blinding rage because he dared to question my plan or tell me to put the brakes on. 

So the energy never dropped, it never went away during the day, it just... it just mutated sometimes. If everyone stayed out of my way, I was on top of the world, sketching and planning and feeling invincible. But the second a coworker questioned me or told me to slow down? Boom. I’d bite their head off. Because how dare they, you know? How dare they try to slow down someone who's about to change everything? I remember Kevin just staring at me, totally shocked, holding this bag of mulch, and I didn't even care that I'd just screamed at him over nothing. I just grabbed another bag and kept moving. So yeah, always fired up, but sometimes it was a really angry, irritable kind of fire if anyone tried to stop me.
Did you ever feel like you were back to your normal self during those two weeks when you were working on the park project?

Normal? No... no way. Not even for a second, doc. I mean, if you think about it, what even is normal, right? Normal for me was, like I was saying earlier, dragging myself out of bed after hitting snooze five times, worrying about the transmission on my truck slipping, worrying about the rain ruining our mowing schedule, just... just being another guy hauling dirt and laying sod. 

But this whole fired-up, overconfident stretch we’ve been talking about? It started the exact moment I decided I was going to completely remake myself for that park pitch. I remember it so clearly. I literally took all my old, messy, half-baked sketches that I'd done on the back of receipts and napkins, and I just tossed them in the dumpster behind the shop. Then I drove straight to the office supply store on my lunch break—I was still wearing my muddy boots, tracking dirt all over their clean floors, not even caring what the cashier or anyone else thought of me—and I bought all new grid paper, the good drafting pens, the thick binders. Because I was reinventing myself. I was remaking who I was so I could match the massive scale of this pitch. I wasn't just a groundskeeper anymore; I was a visionary.

And once I flipped that switch, once that remaking process started, there was absolutely no going back to "normal." It was just full throttle, all day, every day. The whole thing lasted about two weeks. Two solid weeks of just being... elevated. Unstoppable. I didn't wake up on day five or day ten and think, "Oh, I'm just a landscaper again." No, I was the architect of the future for fourteen straight days. Every single minute of it. It just kept going and going, the momentum just building and building on itself for those two weeks, right up until I finally crashed. 

And man, when I crashed, I really crashed. But before that happened, before the bottom completely fell out from under me, there was zero dipping back into my normal self. It was just two weeks of pure, uninterrupted fire.
Did you notice any change in your mood or energy level right before everything fell apart and you crashed?

Change? No... no, doc, that's the craziest part of the whole thing. There was absolutely no warning light. No sputtering engine, to use a truck metaphor, you know? I didn't feel myself slowing down or getting tired or... or anything like that. I was going full throttle right up until the exact second I wasn't. 

I remember it was a Tuesday night. Yeah, Tuesday, because we had just finished that nightmare mulch job on 4th Street I was telling you about. I got home and I didn't even shower. I just kicked off my muddy boots by the door—left dirt all over the linoleum, which I usually hate doing, but right then I didn't care because I had to get back to the plans. I went straight to the kitchen table. I had all my thick binders spread out everywhere, the good grid paper, my drafting pens lined up perfectly on the right side of the desk. I was in the middle of drawing this really intricate elevation for a tiered water feature that was going to connect the north and south ends of the park... 

And I was feeling it, man. The energy was just pumping through me. My brain was firing on all cylinders, same as it had been for the last fourteen days. And then... I don't even know how to explain it. It was just like someone walked over and pulled the main power plug out of the wall. Just... snap. Complete darkness. 

One second I'm this visionary architect of the future, and the very next second I'm just a guy sitting in a dirty kitchen staring at a piece of paper, and I don't even know what I'm looking at anymore. It wasn't like a slow leak in a tire where you kind of feel the steering get mushy before it goes flat, where you have time to pull over. It was a blowout at eighty miles an hour. I just sat there at the table, holding this pen, and suddenly it felt like the pen weighed fifty pounds. My arm was just dead. And all those massive, world-changing ideas? Gone. Just completely empty. 

I didn't feel my mood dropping beforehand, I didn't feel myself getting sad or irritable or anything that would tell me the ride was over. I remember looking at the microwave clock, it was like 11:34 PM, and I just put my head down on the table right on top of all those expensive drawings. I didn't even have the energy to move to the bed. So no, I didn't see it coming at all. Not even a hint. If I had, maybe I could have braced for the impact, you know? Put my hands up or something. But there was nothing. Just... boom. Over.
After you crashed and the energy was gone, did you feel sad or depressed?

Sad? Depressed? Man... "sad" is like when your truck breaks down or a job gets rained out. What I felt... what I'm feeling right now... it’s so much heavier than that. It's like being buried alive in wet concrete. 

And the thing you really gotta understand, doc, is that it didn't just start when the lights went out at that kitchen table. It’s not like my life was totally fine and then I just got sad because my park project idea fizzled out. Honestly? This... this depression, this dark, suffocating cloud... it’s been hanging over me for about a year now. A whole solid year. For twelve months, I’ve just been dragging myself through the days, feeling like I've got a hundred-pound sack of wet sand strapped to my back. Just slogging through the mowing routes, staring at the grass, trying not to let the other guys on the crew see how completely empty and hollowed out I felt inside. 

That's why those two weeks of feeling so fired up and invincible were so crazy to me. Because for a second there, I actually thought I had finally outrun it, you know? I thought, "This is it, I've remade myself, I've beat this thing that's been dragging me down all year." 

But then I crashed. And when I woke up the next morning with my face pressed against all those expensive grid papers I bought... man. The darkness didn't just come back. It came back with a vengeance. It was waiting for me. And this latest crash... it is the worst it has ever gotten. I mean, the absolute bottom of the pit. Before, during that whole past year I was depressed, I could at least fake it. I could at least put the truck in drive and push a mower around and pretend to be a functioning human being. But since this crash? There's no faking anything. I just look at the dirt on my boots and I can't even figure out the point of untying the laces. It’s just this crushing, pitch-black hole, and it’s deeper and heavier than it’s ever been in my entire life. I don't even know how to explain how bad it hurts just to exist right now.
Did you feel like you had a lot less energy after you crashed?

Less energy? Doc... I mean... I guess? But "less energy" makes it sound like I just need a good night's sleep or something. It makes it sound like a normal thing. And I don't... I really don't even know if I'd call it having "less" energy, because that implies there's still a little bit left in the tank, you know? Like when the gas light comes on in the work truck, but you know you can still coast another twenty miles to the Exxon station. This wasn't coasting. This was the whole engine dropping out onto the asphalt. 

Usually, if I'm just low on energy, I know how to fix it. I stop at the convenience store on Route 9, I grab two of those massive energy drinks—the ones with the green monster claws on the can—and I just force myself through the day. I’ve done that a million times when we’re behind schedule on a commercial property and the grass is knee-high and the sun is just beating down on you. You just grit your teeth and push. 

But after that Tuesday night? After I crashed at the kitchen table? I couldn't even tell you what energy feels like anymore. I remember waking up the next morning, still in my dirty work clothes, and I just stared at the coffee maker on the counter. I just looked at the empty glass pot. And I started thinking about the physical steps it would take to make a cup. Opening the little plastic drawer, pulling out a paper filter, scooping the grounds, filling the reservoir with water... and it was like I was calculating the physics of building a skyscraper. It was impossible. My arms felt like they were made of lead. I couldn't even lift my hand to scratch my face. 

So I don't know if I'd say I noticed having "less energy" because... I don't know, it's more like the concept of energy just stopped existing for me altogether. It’s like when you go to start a weed whacker, and you pull the cord, and the cord just snaps right off in your hand. You're just standing there holding a frayed piece of string, and the machine is just dead on the grass. There's no spark, no sputtering, nothing. So, I guess I don't really have a good answer for you on that one, other than saying there's just absolutely nothing left to even measure.
After you crashed, did you ever feel extremely irritable or angry for no reason?

After? No... no, doc. After I hit that wall at the kitchen table, I didn't have the energy to be mad. Being angry takes fuel, you know? It takes heat. And I'm just cold and empty right now. I couldn't even muster up the energy to be mad if someone backed a riding mower right over my foot. 

But... if you're asking about before I crashed? Like, during those fourteen days when I was running on all cylinders? Yeah. Yeah, that's a whole different story. 

It's weird because mostly I felt so good, you know? I felt completely fired up and just... I don't know, almost bigger than myself. Like I was this giant walking among regular people who just couldn't see the world the way I was seeing it. I had all these massive plans for the commercial routes and the park project, and I was moving at lightspeed. But the second—and I mean the literal millisecond—that somebody got in my way or tried to pump the brakes? Man, I would just explode. 

Like, we were doing that 4th Street mulch job I mentioned earlier, right? And one of the guys on my crew, Mark, he just made some offhand comment. I was tearing open these heavy bags of dark brown mulch, throwing them around like they weighed nothing, and he just told me I was going too fast and to maybe slow down and grab some water. Just normal coworker stuff, right? Just a guy looking out for his crewmate so I don't drop dead of heatstroke. 

But I just lost it. I snapped at him way, way harder than made any sense at all. I started yelling at him right there in front of the client's office windows. I told him he had no vision, that he was dragging me down, that if he couldn't keep up with my plan he should just go sit in the truck. Just really nasty, aggressive stuff over absolutely nothing. Because in my head, I was on this totally different, elevated level, and him telling me to slow down or questioning my layout for the flower beds... it was like an insult to my whole existence. I just couldn't handle anyone getting in the way of the momentum. 

So yeah, before the crash, the anger was definitely there. I was a powder keg if you didn't agree with my plans. But like I said... after the crash? Nothing. All that fire just turned to ash.
Did you notice yourself becoming more productive or achieving more in the days leading up to when you crashed?

Productive? Oh man, productive doesn't even begin to cover it. It was like I had this massive, industrial-grade motor running inside my chest and someone had just completely cut the brake lines. 

Normally, you know, getting up at 5 AM for a landscaping route is a total drag. You hit snooze three times, you drag yourself to the coffee pot, you just sort of dread the heat. But during those two weeks? I was up way before daylight. I'm talking 3:30, 4:00 in the morning, and my eyes would just snap open, wide awake, completely wired. I’d be out in the driveway in the pitch black with a headlamp on, loading up the tools, organizing the trailer, checking the oil on the trimmers, sharpening the mower blades until they were like razors. I was doing all this maintenance before the birds were even up. 

And then, before the rest of the crew even pulled into the yard, I was sitting in the cab of my truck with the dome light on, just furiously sketching out these massive, elaborate layouts for the landscape beds on that park project I was talking about. I was mapping out the exact square footage, figuring out the soil amendments, and pricing out all these native plants. I got obsessed with the native stuff—coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, switchgrass, blue fescue—calculating the exact wholesale cost down to the penny and leaving voicemails for the nurseries at like 5:30 in the morning. I had this whole binder going.

And the craziest part was that then I'd go out and work a full day. I mean a real, ten or twelve-hour day of brutal manual labor in the sun. Edging, mowing, laying down sod, hauling heavy debris. By 5 or 6 PM, the rest of the guys on the crew are just dead on their feet, right? They're packing up, begging to go home and just collapse on the couch. But me? After a full day outside sweating buckets, I still felt like I had to keep going. I wasn't even breathing hard. I’d get home and instead of taking my boots off, I’d just start pacing the house, or I'd go out and start tearing up my own front yard to put in a new retaining wall, or I'd be back at the kitchen table drafting more blueprints until two in the morning. I just couldn't turn the switch off. It felt like there physically weren't enough hours in the day for everything my brain was telling my hands to build. So yeah, I was getting more done in twenty-four hours than I usually do in a whole month. easily.
Did you feel like you were coming up with more innovative or creative ideas in the days leading up to when you crashed?

Creative? Man, it wasn't just creative, it was like a floodgate opened up and the dam completely washed away. I wasn't just having an idea here or there, my head was running so fast... just constantly, constantly spinning. 

I had this cheap little spiral notebook I usually keep in the center console of the work truck—you know, the kind you buy for a buck at the drugstore just to track mileage or write down a supply run to the hardware store. But during those days? I was just tearing through it. I was filling pages and pages in that notebook. Front and back, in the margins, everywhere, just scribbling like a madman. 

My brain was just firing off these massive plant lists—like, exactly how many flats of impatiens and hostas we'd need for the medians downtown, mixed with, you know, these huge, elaborate park layouts I was designing in my head. I was even coming up with slogans! Like, actual advertising slogans for the company to paint on the side of the enclosed trailers, trying to figure out exactly who I needed to impress to get the big municipal contracts. I was thinking about the city councilmen, the zoning board guys, the commercial property managers, mapping out exactly what I'd say to them to completely blow their minds and revolutionize how they thought about green spaces. 

But the wildest part was... no matter how fast I wrote, no matter how many pages I filled with these park layouts and plant lists and marketing ideas, I still felt behind. Like my hand physically could not move fast enough to catch everything spilling out of my brain. I’d be sitting there scribbling furiously against the steering wheel, and my thoughts were already ten steps ahead of what the pen was doing. It was just... it was relentless, doc. There were so many ideas hitting me all at once that even when I was writing non-stop, I just couldn't get it all down fast enough.
Did you experience any periods of significantly elevated or irritable mood that lasted for most of the day for at least one week?

Oh, definitely more than a week, doc. It was... well, if I really sit down and trace it back to when the engine really caught fire, it was a solid two weeks. Fourteen days straight of just being completely wired and running hot all day long. 

It all really kicked off when I started remaking myself for that big park pitch I was telling you about. I just woke up one morning and decided I wasn't just gonna be some guy on a crew hauling mulch anymore, I was gonna be the guy running the whole show. So I started totally reinventing how I presented myself, you know? I started wearing these crisp collared shirts under my work gear, practicing my handshakes in the rearview mirror of the truck, just completely hyping myself up into this totally overconfident, unstoppable force. I was walking onto residential job sites feeling like I owned the dirt I was standing on, ready to take over the whole municipal landscaping market. 

And that whole stretch—that fired-up, untouchable feeling where I was just buzzing out of my skin and snapping at anyone who got in my way—it didn't quit. Not for a single afternoon. It didn't matter if it was raining or if we were doing a brutal twelve-hour shift pulling up dead sod. I was just riding that massive, arrogant high for about two solid weeks. Fourteen days of just pure, uninterrupted momentum... right up until the exact second my brain just gave out and I crashed hard at the kitchen table.
Did you experience any periods of significantly elevated or irritable mood that lasted for most of the day for at least four consecutive days?

Well, yeah, like I was just saying, it was a solid fourteen days of it, so four consecutive days is a given. It was every single day right up until I finally crashed. 

And "elevated" is a good word for it, because I felt so incredibly fired up. Honestly, I felt almost bigger than myself, if that makes any sense? Like I was ten feet tall and bulletproof, just stomping around these high-end residential job sites like I owned the entire neighborhood. I felt like I could lift a riding mower with my bare hands. 

But the flip side of being that dialed in is that I had absolutely zero patience for anybody else. None. Because my brain is operating on this totally different, superior level, right?
